claims.claim: **Four organ systems are involved:** eye (ectopia lentis, severe myopia), skeleton (marfanoid habitus, osteoporosis), central nervous system (developmental delay, seizures, psychiatric problems) and vascular system (thromboembolism).
claims.source_text: EYE: ectopia lentis and/or severe myopia Skeleton: excessive height and length of the limbs ('marfanoid' habitus), osteoporosis and bone deformities, such as pectus excavatum or carinatum, genu valgum and scoliosis Central nervous system: developmental delay/intellectual disability, seizures, psychiatric and behavioural problems and extrapyramidal signs Vascular system: thromboembolism
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Children tend to present with developmental delay and lens dislocation; adults after a vascular event.** Marfan syndrome and prothrombotic disorders are key differentials.
claims.source_text: Children are more likely to present with developmental delay and ectopia lentis. Adults are more likely to be diagnosed following vascular events. … The differential diagnosis of the presenting features is very broad and includes Marfan syndrome and prothrombotic disorders
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) is the frontline test.** Pyridoxine or fortified multivitamins taken before testing can mask mild disease.
claims.source_text: Plasma total homocysteine (tHcy) should be the frontline test for diagnosis of CBS deficiency. … The diagnosis can be masked in patients with mild disease who are taking pyridoxine or pyridoxine-fortified multivitamins and foods prior to biochemical testing.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Separate plasma within one hour of venepuncture.** Low or low-normal methionine, or raised methylmalonic acid, points to a cause other than CBS deficiency (such as B12 or folate deficiency).
claims.source_text: Plasma should ideally be separated from whole blood within one hour of venepuncture … Decreased or low normal plasma Met, elevated plasma cystathionine and/or elevated plasma or urinary methylmalonic acid concentrations suggest causes of hyperhomocysteinemia other than CBS deficiency.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Confirm with CBS enzyme activity and/or CBS gene analysis;** neither detects every case. When an index case is found, offer biochemical screening to at-risk relatives.
claims.source_text: CBS deficiency should be confirmed by measurement of cystathionine synthase activity in fibroblasts or plasma and/or by mutation analysis of the CBS gene. Neither technique can be relied on to demonstrate abnormalities in all cases. … When an index case is detected, screening of at-risk family members should be offered using biochemical testing
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Targets:** tHcy below 50 μmol/L in pyridoxine-responsive patients; in pyridoxine-unresponsive patients the guideline recommends keeping tHcy below 100 μmol/L, with normal methionine and nutrition.
claims.source_text: Treatment aims to lower the plasma tHcy concentration to a safe level whilst maintaining normal nutrition, including normal concentrations of methionine and other essential AA. In pyridoxine-responsive patients the target for plasma tHcy should be <50 μmol/L. … We recommend keeping tHcy levels below 100 μmol/L but this may need revision when very long term data become available.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Test pyridoxine responsiveness after infancy with 10 mg/kg/day (maximum 500 mg/day) for 6 weeks,** measuring tHcy at least twice before and twice on treatment, with normal protein intake and folate given. Below 50 μmol/L on pyridoxine means fully responsive; a fall of more than 20% that stays above 50 means add diet and/or betaine.
claims.source_text: To assess pyridoxine responsiveness after infancy, we recommend giving 10 mg/kg/day pyridoxine up to a maximum of 500 mg/day for 6 weeks; the plasma tHcy concentration should be measured at least twice before treatment and twice on treatment. The test should not be done if the patient is catabolic. The protein intake should be normal, folate supplements should be given and vitamin B 12 deficiency should be corrected prior to testing. Patients who achieve plasma tHcy levels below 50 μmol/l on pyridoxine are clearly responsive and do not need any other treatment. If the tHcy falls >20 % but remains above 50 μmol/L, additional treatment should be considered (i.e. diet and/or betaine). If tHcy falls by <20 % on pyridoxine, the patient is likely to be unresponsive.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Babies found by newborn screening rarely respond;** test them with 100 mg/day for 2 weeks.
claims.source_text: Patients detected by newborn screening rarely respond to pyridoxine and, in this group, we recommend using a relatively high dose (100 mg/day) for a shorter period (2 weeks).
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Use the lowest effective pyridoxine dose,** up to 10 mg/kg/day, avoiding more than 500 mg/day: long-term doses above 900 mg/day cause peripheral neuropathy. Do not continue pyridoxine without a biochemical response.
claims.source_text: For long-term treatment, the pyridoxine dose should be the lowest that achieves the biochemical targets (plasma total homocysteine <50 μmol/L). We recommend using doses up to 10 mg/kg/day and avoiding doses above 500 mg/day. … Peripheral neuropathy is the most important adverse effect of pyridoxine. It has been reported in a number of patients treated with long-term high doses of pyridoxine >900 mg/day. … There is no evidence that long-term pyridoxine is beneficial if there is no biochemical response in a properly conducted test.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give all patients adequate folate;** monitor B12 and supplement if deficient.
claims.source_text: All patients should receive adequate folate supplementation. Vitamin B 12 should be monitored and supplemented if deficient.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider diet for every patient not at target on pyridoxine alone.** Most pyridoxine-unresponsive patients need a diet very low in natural protein plus a **methionine-free amino acid mixture**, for life.
claims.source_text: Dietary treatment should be considered for all patients with CBS deficiency unless target Hcy levels are achieved entirely by pyridoxine supplementation. Diet may be used either as a sole treatment or adjunctive therapy along with pyridoxine and/or betaine. Most pyridoxine-unresponsive patients require a diet that is very low in natural protein, with supplements of a Met-free L-AA mixture. Lifelong treatment is required.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Most need a low-methionine diet with a cystine-enriched, methionine-free supplement;** some partial responders manage with milder protein restriction and no supplement. The degree of restriction is set by each patient's tHcy and methionine.
claims.source_text: The majority of patients on dietary treatment require a low Met diet with a cystine-enriched, Met-free L-AA supplement. Some partially pyridoxine-responsive patients benefit from milder protein restriction without Met-free L-AA supplements. … The level of Met or natural protein restriction required varies and is determined for each patient according to their plasma tHcy and Met concentrations.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Betaine is an adjunct** for patients not at target by other means; on its own it seldom reaches target in pyridoxine-unresponsive disease.
claims.source_text: Betaine should be considered as adjunctive treatment in patients who cannot achieve target levels of Hcy by other means. … Betaine treatment alone seldom achieves target Hcy levels in patients with pyridoxine-unresponsive CBS deficiency.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Betaine dosing:** children start at 50 mg/kg twice daily, adults at 3 grams twice daily, adjusted to response; exceeding 150-200 mg/kg/day is unlikely to help. Higher doses cause a fishy odour; cerebral oedema is very rare.
claims.source_text: For children, the initial betaine dose is 50 mg/kg twice daily. For adults, the starting dose is 3 grams twice a day. The dose and frequency are adjusted according to response. There is unlikely to be any benefit in exceeding a dose of 150-200 mg/kg/day. … Generally betaine is well tolerated and safe. Higher doses have been associated with a fishy odor. Cerebral edema is a very rare side effect.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Monitor tHcy, plasma amino acids (including methionine), B12 and folate in everyone;** six-monthly tHcy may be enough for fully pyridoxine-responsive adults, but children on diet need far more frequent checks. Measure B12 and folate annually.
claims.source_text: In adult patients who are fully pyridoxine-responsive it may be adequate to monitor tHcy levels every six months. In contrast, in children on dietary treatment for pyridoxine-unresponsive CBS deficiency, tHcy and Met will need to be monitored much more frequently. … The serum vitamin B12 and folate levels should be measured annually
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **DEXA every 3-5 years from adolescence;** MRI only with abnormal neurological signs.
claims.source_text: Bone density scans (DEXA) should be done every 3-5 years from adolescence with additional scans in individuals who have frequent fractures and/or low vitamin D levels. Neuroimaging (MRI) is only indicated in individuals who have abnormal neurological signs.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Venous thromboembolism risk may reach 50% by age 30 in untreated pyridoxine-unresponsive patients.** Lowering tHcy is the most important protection; keep patients hydrated. Poorly controlled patients or those with a past event may need antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy.
claims.source_text: In untreated pyridoxine unresponsive patients, the risk may be as high as 50 % by 30 years of age. … Prevention of dehydration is important. Patients who are poorly controlled or have had a vascular event may warrant additional treatment with anti-platelet drugs or anticoagulants, according to local guidelines. … lowering the plasma tHcy is the single most important factor in reducing the risk of thromboembolic disease
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Avoid oestrogen-containing contraceptives.**
claims.source_text: Estrogen containing contraceptives should be avoided due to the increased risk of thrombosis.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Pregnancy:** low molecular weight heparin in the third trimester (possibly throughout) and for at least 6 weeks postpartum; review diet often as methionine needs rise, and cut methionine back to pre-pregnancy levels after delivery. Give at least 400 micrograms folate.
claims.source_text: Anticoagulant therapy in the form of low molecular weight heparin is recommended during the third trimester (and maybe throughout pregnancy) and for at least 6 weeks postpartum. Met requirements often increase through pregnancy; it is important that the dietary management is regularly reviewed with frequent biochemical monitoring. After delivery, the Met intake should be reduced to no more than pre-pregnancy levels. … All pregnant patients should receive folate supplementation (at least 400 micrograms)
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **During intercurrent illness, continue all treatment** (pyridoxine, betaine, amino acid mixture, energy) and avoid dehydration and immobility.
claims.source_text: During intercurrent illness, patients should continue their regular treatment (such as pyridoxine, betaine, their L-AA mixture and adequate energy). Dehydration and immobilization should be avoided to reduce the risk of thromboembolic disease.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Surgery:** optimise control first, keep hydrated with IV fluids, use mechanical thromboprophylaxis and early mobilisation, LMWH if immobilisation is prolonged, and **avoid nitrous oxide**, which raises homocysteine.
claims.source_text: Surgery and anaesthesia pose an additional risk of thrombosis in CBS deficiency. Biochemical control, dietary management and nutrition should be optimised before elective procedures. Hydration should be maintained with intravenous fluids. Standard anti-thrombotic measures such as elastic stockings, pneumatic leg compression systems and early mobilization should be followed during and after surgery. Low molecular weight heparin is recommended in cases of prolonged immobilisation. Nitrous oxide increases Hcy concentrations and should be avoided.
claims.locator: Morris AAM, Kožich V, Santra S, et al. (E-HOD consortium), Journal of Inherited Metabolic Disease, 'Guidelines for the diagnosis and management of cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency', vol. 40, pp. 49–74, published 2017 (online 2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5203861/, retrieved 2026-09-23
